lesson.title: CSMA/CD: Catching Collisions in the Act
lesson.summary: Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection, the access method of classic Ethernet, has a transmitting station keep monitoring the cable while it sends so it can detect a collision immediately, abort the wasted transmission, and back off, rather than sending a full useless frame to completion.
lesson.body:
Plain CSMA reduces collisions but, once one happens, both stations typically keep transmitting their entire frame to completion before finding out, via a missing acknowledgment, that the effort was wasted. CSMA with Collision Detection, CSMA/CD, closes that gap for media where it is physically possible: while transmitting, a station continues to listen to the cable, comparing what it is putting onto the wire against what it actually senses there. On a shared coaxial or twisted pair segment, a collision produces a voltage level distinguishable from either station's clean signal, so a transmitting station can recognize, within a fairly short delay, that a collision is underway.

As soon as a station detects a collision, it does two things immediately: it stops sending the actual frame data, since that data is already corrupted and useless, and it transmits a short jam signal, deliberately noisy bits meant to ensure that every other station on the segment also notices the collision, even ones whose own signal might otherwise have looked clean to them at that instant. Only after jamming does the station give up the channel and schedule a retransmission attempt.

The retransmission timing uses binary exponential backoff rather than a simple fixed random delay. After the first collision on a given frame, the station picks a random number of slot times to wait from the set 0 or 1, doubling the range after each successive collision on the same frame, 0 through 3 after the second collision, 0 through 7 after the third, and so on, up to a capped maximum, before giving up and reporting a failure to the upper layer after a set number of attempts, traditionally sixteen in classic Ethernet. This growing randomization spreads out retries under contention: a network with many stations repeatedly colliding backs off more aggressively than one with an occasional lone collision, which keeps the channel usable instead of collapsing into a storm of immediate retries.

There is a hard constraint tying frame size to network size that CSMA/CD depends on for correctness: a station must still be transmitting at the moment it could possibly learn about a collision, or it will never detect one at all, and could go on believing its frame was sent cleanly when it was not. Concretely, the frame transmission time must be at least twice the maximum one way propagation delay across the network, since that is the worst case round trip time for a collision signal to travel to the far end and the resulting jam or corrupted signal to propagate back. This is exactly why classic Ethernet specified a minimum frame size of 64 bytes together with a maximum cable span: shrink the frame or stretch the cable beyond what that relationship allows, and a station could finish transmitting, believing it succeeded, before a collision it caused even reaches it.

CSMA/CD was the defining access method of Ethernet over shared coaxial cable and shared hubs, but it became largely irrelevant once switched, full duplex Ethernet became standard: a switch gives every port its own dedicated collision domain, and full duplex means a station can send and receive simultaneously on separate wire pairs, so there is no shared medium left to sense or collide on in the first place. Modern Ethernet still lists CSMA/CD in its formal name and standard for historical and half duplex compatibility reasons, but the collision detection logic is largely dormant on typical switched networks today.
